# Symmetric triangle chains: shared-tilt sectors and an exact lattice correction

Let T=conv(0,e1,e2), V=|T|. Let m>=0 and let the actual fibers at
integer bases -m,...,m be r_k T, where r_{-k}=r_k>0 and the sequence
is concave. Put R=r_0 and M=sum_{k=-m}^m r_k^2. Its concave linear
interpolation gives a full convex body when m>=1; when m=0 only the
fiber statement below is relevant. At the actual peak centroid

    y=(0,R/3,R/3)

all through-point caps can be reduced, without increasing any fiber's
mass, to positive continuous normals by the previously proved
common-vertex-simplex-positive-normal-reduction.md. Coordinate exchange
and positive scaling then give the continuous normal (a,1-a),
1/2<=a<=1, and one shared integer tilt beta. All formulas here keep
that shared tilt. We do not prove the desired inequality for every
intermediate a, nor infer general OC from these results.

There are three conclusions.

1. For every a in [2/3,1], the minimizing tilt is exactly beta=0:

    inf_beta cap(a,beta)/V
       = a/(2a-1) sum_k (r_k-R/(3a))_+^2.                (1)

   Thus this all-length sector has no loss from independently
   optimizing paired tilts. The formula includes every beta and
   oblique cap in the sector.

2. For the equal continuous normal a=1/2, every shared tilt satisfies

    cap(1/2,beta)/V >= (2/9)M + R^2/243.               (2)

   The quantitative positive term comes from an exact discrete
   trapezoid correction; no sum has been replaced by an integral.

3. In the remaining sector, the exact fixed-normal pair costs and
   a shared-tilt quadratic penalty are given in Sections 2 and 5.
   The preferred positive shifts decrease with pair distance,
   whereas actual shifts increase, a concrete compatibility constraint.

## 1. The triangular tail and the exact pair regimes

Write t=R/3. For 1/2<a<1 define the cap area divided by V as

    F_{a,r}(s)=r^2,                              s<=0;
    F_{a,r}(s)=r^2-s^2/[a(1-a)],                0<=s<=(1-a)r;
    F_{a,r}(s)=(ar-s)^2/[a(2a-1)],             (1-a)r<=s<=ar;
    F_{a,r}(s)=0,                              s>=ar.       (3)

The expressions agree at their endpoints and their first derivatives
agree. At a=1 use F=(r-s)_+^2 clipped above by r^2. At a=1/2 use
F=r^2-4s^2 on 0<=s<=r/2, clipped above and below.

The pair at bases +/-h contributes

    P_{a,r_h}(h|beta|),
    P_{a,r}(s)=F_{a,r}(t-s)+F_{a,r}(t+s), s>=0.       (4)

Every cut line has zero area, so these are closed-cap formulas.

Here is the short complete fixed-normal minimization. Normalize the
three vertex heights to (0,c,1), where c=(1-a)/a, and the threshold to
q=t/(ar). The normalized upper tail is 1-x^2/c below c and
(1-x)^2/(1-c) above c, clipped outside [0,1]. For two opposite shifts:

* Both cuts in the lower piece give a concave quadratic in the shift.
* Both cuts in the upper piece give a convex quadratic whose only
  interior minimum is at shift zero.
* A full cap costs at least one; a full/empty plateau costs one.
* An empty cap paired with a proper cap has increasing cost as the
  nonnegative shift increases.
* A proper straddling stationary minimum exists only when c>1/2
  and 1/2<=q<=c. Its shift is (c-q)/(2c-1), and its value is

      1-(2q-1)^2/(2c-1).                            (5)

The stationary point lies in the straddling regime exactly under
these inequalities: its lower threshold is c(2q-1)/(2c-1)>=0,
its upper threshold is <=1, and both lie on their stated sides of c.
If c<=1/2, the straddling quadratic is concave, or linear at equality,
and supplies no smaller interior minimum. At regime endpoints, the
first derivatives agree, so no further minimum is omitted. This proves
the complete minimization. Degenerate heights a=1/2,1 follow directly
from the displayed one-piece tails, without a limiting assumption.

## 2. Exact fixed-normal pair floors

Because r<=R, for a>=2/3 one has t>=(1-a)r and
F_{a,r}(t)<=F_{a,R}(t)<=R^2/2, with the scale-correct assertion
F_{a,r}(t)<=r^2/2 following by threshold monotonicity in t/r.
There is no straddling minimum in Section 1. Therefore

    min_{s>=0} P_{a,r}(s)=2F_{a,r}(t), a>=2/3.       (6)

Each pair attains (6) at the SAME original beta=0. The own fiber
is independent of beta. Formula (3) now proves (1), including a=1.
No concavity beyond r<=R is needed for this sector identity.

For 1/2<a<2/3 put

    c_a=t/a,       rho_a=t/(1-a).

The complete pair minimum, divided by V as throughout, is

    Q_a(r)=0,                                  0<=r<=c_a;
    Q_a(r)=2(ar-t)^2/[a(2a-1)],                 c_a<=r<=rho_a;
    Q_a(r)=r^2-(2t-ar)^2/[a(2-3a)],              rho_a<=r<=R.  (7)

Indeed, below rho_a the normalized threshold is beyond the mode,
and the zero-shift value is at most r^2. Above rho_a, it lies between
one half and the mode, so (5) applies. The difference between the
zero-shift pair value and (5), after multiplication by c(2c-1), is
2(c-q)^2, hence nonnegative. The stationary value is also at most one.
These checks compare all candidates from Section 1.

The limits at the adjoining r-values agree. At a=1/2 the exact formula is

    Q_{1/2}(r)=8t(r-2t)_+ .                         (8)

For r<=2t, zero shift excludes both caps. For r>=2t, the upper-support
contact shift r/2-t gives r^2-(4t-r)^2=8t(r-2t); r<=R=3t ensures the
normalized threshold is at least 2/3, so this is the global pair minimum.
The own-fiber cap in this direction is exactly 5R^2/9.

## 3. A corrected hinge inequality for every symmetric concave sequence

The exact scalar statement is

    sum_k (r_k-2R/3)_+ >= M/(6R) - 13R/162.          (9)

This includes m=0. Its weaker version with correction R/12 also follows,
since 13/162<1/12. The uncorrected assertion is false: for the positive
concave sequence (1/3,2/3,1,2/3,1/3), its two sides would be 1/3 and19/54.

Normalize R=1, and put

    f(v)=6(v-2/3)_+-v^2, 0<=v<=1.                  (10)

We prove sum_k f(r_k)>=-13/27. The primitive A(v)=integral_0^v f
is nonpositive everywhere and A(1)=0. Below 2/3 it is -v^3/3.
Above 2/3 it is 3(v-2/3)^2-v^3/3. Here f is strictly increasing
from -4/9 to1 and crosses zero once, so A first decreases and then
increases to its value zero at1, establishing the sign claim.

Let r(z) be the linear interpolation of r_0,...,r_m on [0,m].
Symmetry and concavity give 1=r_0>=r_1>=...>=r_m=b>0, with
nondecreasing drops delta_i=r_i-r_{i+1}>=0. On a nonconstant segment,
the change of variable v=r(z) gives inverse-radius density1/delta_i.
As v increases this density is nondecreasing, since the drops increase
outward. Extend the density by zero on [0,b). Every nonnegative
nondecreasing finite step function on [0,1] is a positive linear
combination of upper-interval indicators 1_[c,1]. Each such interval
has integral of f equal to -A(c)>=0. Initial constant segments can
only have value1, contributing their length times f(1)=1. Therefore

    integral_0^m f(r(z)) dz >=0.                    (11)

This proves the comparison directly for the actual polygonal roof;
no approximation, derivative of an inverse at a plateau, or infinite
step decomposition is needed. If every drop is zero, the assertion
is immediate.

On a unit interpolation cell, the trapezoid error for -r(z)^2 is
exactly -delta_i^2/6. The function (r(z)-2/3)_+ is convex on that
cell, so its trapezoid error is nonnegative. Consequently the total
trapezoid sum T_f satisfies

    T_f - integral_0^m f(r(z)) dz >= -sum_i delta_i^2/6.

The full symmetric discrete sum is exactly 2T_f+f(b). Since the drops
are nonnegative and sum to1-b, it follows that

    sum_{k=-m}^m f(r_k)
       >= f(b) - (1/3)sum_i delta_i^2
       >= f(b) - (1-b)^2/3.                         (12)

For0<=b<=2/3, the last expression is -b^2-(1-b)^2/3,
a concave quadratic whose minimum over the interval is at an endpoint;
the values are -1/3 and -13/27. For2/3<=b<=1, its derivative is
6-2b+2(1-b)/3>0, so the minimum is again -13/27 at b=2/3.
This proves (9) after undoing the normalization. For m=0, the
sum is f(1)=1 and the same claimed lower bound holds separately.

## 4. All shared tilts in the equal-normal sector

Apply (8) to every reflected pair and keep the exact own contribution:

    cap(1/2,beta)/V
      >=5R^2/9 + sum_{h=1}^m (8R/3)(r_h-2R/3)_+
       =(4R/3)sum_{k=-m}^m(r_k-2R/3)_+ +R^2/9.

Using (9) gives

    cap/V >=(2/9)M - (26/243)R^2 +(27/243)R^2
           =(2/9)M+R^2/243,

which is (2). Independent pair floors are only lower bounds here;
we do not assert one beta realizes all of them. That possible mismatch
can only improve the proven original cap bound. Closed vertical caps
also exceed the target: by symmetry they capture the whole own fiber
and one complete member of every pair, at least M/2 volume units.

## 5. The remaining sector retains an explicit shared-tilt penalty

For1/2<a<2/3, while the two proper cuts in a pair straddle its mode,
there is the exact identity

    P_{a,r}(s)=J_a(r)+K_a(s-s_a(r))^2,
    J_a(r)=r^2-(2t-ar)^2/[a(2-3a)],
    K_a=(2-3a)/[a(2a-1)(1-a)]>0,
    s_a(r)=a[(1-a)r-t]/(2-3a).                      (13)

It follows by expanding (3), with t-s in its lower proper piece and
t+s in its upper proper piece. The straddling interval, including its
null-boundary endpoints, is exactly

    |t-(1-a)r| <= s <= min(t,ar-t),

when this interval is nonempty. Identity (13) also holds when the
formal stationary shift s_a(r) is negative; then it does not represent
an attained pair minimum over nonnegative s.

For any specified set I of reflected distances whose actual cuts are
all in these regimes, their combined contribution is

    sum_{h in I} J_a(r_h)
       +K_a sum_{h in I}(h|beta|-s_a(r_h))^2.         (14)

Writing B=sum_I h^2, the last sum equals

    B(|beta|-sum_I h s_a(r_h)/B)^2
       +sum_I s_a(r_h)^2-(sum_I h s_a(r_h))^2/B.      (15)

All terms and the single original beta remain explicit. The preferred
shifts s_a(r_h) are nonincreasing in h; when positive, their ratio to h
is strictly decreasing unless no two positive distances occur. Hence
two distinct positive stationary shifts cannot simultaneously match one
positive beta. Equations (13)-(15) give a precise penalty, but are not
claimed outside their stated regimes. Full/empty transitions cannot
be discarded by extending the quadratic to arbitrarily large beta.

For reference, the high-sector continuous factor obeys

    a/(2a-1)*(1-1/(3a))^3 >=1/4, 2/3<=a<=1.

Its logarithmic derivative has the sign of3a-2, so its minimum occurs
at a=2/3. The subsequently proved and independently audited theorem in
candidate ff51b2f45de7ad0e supplies

    sum(r_j-c)_+^2 >=(1-c/R)^3 M
       +c(R-c)^2/[R(2m+1)].

Applying it at c=R/(3a) to (1) proves that every cap in the complete
high sector has mass strictly greater than V M/4, hence greater than
(2/9)V M. The displayed positive finite-length remainder is retained.
This is a proved dependency, not a replacement of an integer sum by
a continuous integral.
